claim: Kdm6b is more abundantly expressed than Kdm6a and Uty in both palate mesenchymal and epithelial cells.
source: We found that, of these, Kdm6b is more abundantly expressed than Kdm6a and Uty in both palate mesenchymal and epithelial cells, which indicated it might play a critical role in regulating palatogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression pattern evaluation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–F and stated in the text.

claim: Loss of Kdm6b in CNC-derived cells resulted in complete cleft palate in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice with 90% phenotype penetrance.
source: Loss of Kdm6b in CNC-derived cells resulted in complete cleft palate in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice (90% phenotype penetrance, N = 10) and postnatal lethality at newborn stage (100% phenotype penetrance, N = 10) without interrupting expression of other KDM6 family members ( Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mouse models shown in Figure 1A and B, with quantified penetrance.

claim: Loss of Kdm6b in CNC-derived cells resulted in postnatal lethality at newborn stage with 100% phenotype penetrance.
source: Loss of Kdm6b in CNC-derived cells resulted in complete cleft palate in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice (90% phenotype penetrance, N = 10) and postnatal lethality at newborn stage (100% phenotype penetrance, N = 10) without interrupting expression of other KDM6 family members ( Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from mouse models with quantified penetrance.

claim: Loss of Kdm6b in epithelial cells did not lead to obvious defects in the craniofacial region in Krt14Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
source: Interestingly, loss of Kdm6b in epithelial cells did not lead to obvious defects in the craniofacial region in Krt14Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mouse models shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–H.

claim: Kdm6b is specifically required in CNC-derived cells during palatogenesis.
source: These results emphasized that Kdm6b is specifically required in CNC-derived cells during palatogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of phenotypes between Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl and Krt14Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.

claim: The most severe defects in the palatal region of Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice were hypoplastic palatine processes of the maxilla and palatine bones.
source: CT images also confirmed the complete cleft palate phenotype and revealed that the most severe defects in the palatal region of Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice were hypoplastic palatine processes of the maxilla and palatine bones (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by CT imaging data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Kdm6b was efficiently inactivated in CNC-derived cells at E9.5.
source: To evaluate when Kdm6b was inactivated in the CNC-derived cells, we also investigated the expression of Kdm6b at E9.5, well prior to the formation of the palate primordium, and found that Kdm6b was efficiently inactivated in the CNC-derived cells at this stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1O and P).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1O and P.

claim: CNCCs' migration was not adversely affected in Kdm6b mutant mice.
source: The results showed that CNCCs' migration was not adversely affected in Kdm6b mutant mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by tdTomato reporter analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The cleft palate phenotype emerged as early as E14.5 in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
source: Then, we evaluated the process of palatogenesis at different embryonic stages and found that the cleft palate phenotype emerged as early as E14.5 in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis at different embryonic stages shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Kdm6b is not essential for CNCCs entering the pharyngeal arch but is specifically required in regulating post-migratory CNC-derived cells during palatogenesis.
source: These data established that Kdm6b is not essential for CNCCs entering the pharyngeal arch but is specifically required in regulating post-migratory CNC-derived cells during palatogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from migration and palatogenesis data showing normal migration but defects in post-migratory development.

claim: The number of cells positively stained with EdU was significantly increased in the CNC-derived palatal mesenchyme in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice compared to controls after 2 hr of EdU labeling.
source: After 2 hr of EdU labeling, we found that the number of cells positively stained with EdU was significantly increased in the CNC-derived palatal mesenchyme in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice compared to controls (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: The number of Ki67 and EdU double-positive cells was significantly increased in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice after 48 hr of EdU labeling.
source: In addition, after 48 hr of EdU labeling, we found that the number of Ki67 and EdU double-positive cells was significantly increased in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice (Figure 2D–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 2D–H.

claim: Loss of Kdm6b in CNC-derived cells resulted in more cells remaining in the cell cycle and actively proliferating, leading to hyperproliferation of mesenchymal cells in the palatal region.
source: These results indicated that loss of Kdm6b in CNC-derived cells resulted in more cells remaining in the cell cycle and actively proliferating, which further led to hyperproliferation of mesenchymal cells in the palatal region of Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from EdU and Ki67 double-positive cell data.

claim: Palatal mesenchymal cells of Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice showed more expression of β-galactosidase, suggesting increased cellular senescence.
source: Meanwhile, palatal mesenchymal cells of Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice showed more expression of β-galactosidase, which suggested increased cellular senescence in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: There was less expression of Lamin B1 in the palatal mesenchyme of Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice after 48 hr of EdU labeling.
source: After 48 hr of EdU labeling, we found that there was less expression of Lamin B1 in the palatal mesenchyme of Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by Lamin B1 staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–L.

claim: Fewer EdU+ cells expressing Lamin B1 were observed in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice after 48 hr of EdU labeling.
source: More importantly, fewer EdU+ cells expressing Lamin B1 were observed in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–L.

claim: Hyperproliferation may cause increased cellular senescence in palatal mesenchymal cells of Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
source: These data suggested that hyperproliferation may cause increased cellular senescence in palatal mesenchymal cells of Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from β-galactosidase and Lamin B1 data.

claim: There was a decrease in the number of RUNX2+ cells in the palatal mesenchyme at both E13.5 and E14.5 in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice in comparison to the control.
source: There was a decrease in the number of RUNX2+ cells in the palatal mesenchyme at both E13.5 and E14.5 in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice in comparison to the control (Figure 2I–L and Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by RUNX2 immunostaining data shown in Figure 2I–L and Q.

claim: SP7+ cells were decreased in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice at both E14.5 and E15.5.
source: In addition, SP7+ cells were also decreased in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice at both E14.5 and E15.5 (Figure 2M–P and R).
evidence: The claim is supported by SP7 immunostaining data shown in Figure 2M–P and R.

claim: Cells from Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice showed much less calcium deposition than cells from control mice during osteogenic differentiation, indicating a reduction in osteogenic potential.
source: Furthermore, when we induced osteogenic differentiation in palatal mesenchymal cells from E13.5 embryos for 3 weeks, we found that cells from Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice showed much less calcium deposition than cells from control mice, indicating a reduction in osteogenic potential in cells from Kdm6b mutant mice (Figure 2S–W).
evidence: The claim is supported by Alizarin red S staining data shown in Figure 2S–W.

claim: Kdm6b is indispensable for maintaining normal proliferation and differentiation of CNC-derived cells.
source: These results indicated that Kdm6b was indispensable for maintaining normal proliferation and differentiation of CNC-derived cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from proliferation and differentiation marker data.

claim: More genes were downregulated than upregulated in the palatal mesenchyme in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
source: The results showed that more genes were downregulated than upregulated in the palatal mesenchyme in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice (Figure 3A), which is consistent with the function of Kdm6b in removing the repressive mark H3K27me3.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Both IPA and GO analysis indicated that pathways involving Trp53 might be disturbed in the palatal mesenchyme in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
source: Surprisingly, both analyses indicated that pathways involving Trp53 might be disturbed in the palatal mesenchyme in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by IPA and GO analysis shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Trp53 significantly decreased in the palatal region of the Kdm6b mutant mice.
source: We analyzed the expression of Trp53 in our samples and found that it significantly decreased in the palatal region of the Kdm6b mutant mice (Figure 3D–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3D–H.

claim: Kdm6b plays an important role in regulating the P53 pathway in the CNC-derived mesenchyme during palatogenesis.
source: These results indicate that Kdm6b plays an important role in regulating the P53 pathway in the CNC-derived mesenchyme during palatogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from Trp53 expression data and pathway analysis.

claim: DNA damage increased, as indicated by γH2AX expression, in the palatal mesenchyme in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
source: We found that DNA damage increased, as indicated by γH2AX expression, in the palatal mesenchyme in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice (Figure 3I–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by γH2AX immunostaining data shown in Figure 3I–M.

claim: Significantly increased γH2AX foci were observed in the EdU+ cells of Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl palatal mesenchyme.
source: More importantly, we observed significantly increased γH2AX foci in the EdU+ cells of Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl palatal mesenchyme (Figure 3N–R).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 3N–R.

claim: Actively proliferating cells in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice experienced more severe DNA damage compared to those in the control mice, which might be the result of replication stress caused by hyperproliferation.
source: These data indicated that actively proliferating cells in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice experienced more severe DNA damage compared to those in the control mice, which might be the result of replication stress caused by the hyperproliferation we observed in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from EdU and γH2AX co-localization data.

claim: The expression of Trp53 was significantly decreased in cells treated with siRNA after 3 days.
source: qPCR revealed that the expression of Trp53 was significantly decreased in the cells treated with siRNA after 3 days (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The group transfected with siRNA for Trp53 showed a significant increase in EdU+ cells.
source: At the same time, the group transfected with siRNA for Trp53 showed a significant increase in EdU+ cells (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: Significantly increased γH2AX+ cells were observed in the group transfected with siRNA for Trp53.
source: In addition, significantly increased γH2AX+ cells were also observed in the group transfected with siRNA for Trp53 (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by γH2AX immunostaining data shown in Figure 4D–F.

claim: Downregulated expression of Trp53 in the palatal mesenchymal cells is a key factor that led to the hyperproliferation and increased DNA damage observed in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
source: These data suggested that downregulated expression of Trp53 in the palatal mesenchymal cells is a key factor that led to the hyperproliferation and increased DNA damage we observed in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from siRNA knockdown experiments showing similar phenotypes.

claim: Expression of both Runx2 and Sp7 was significantly reduced in the palatal mesenchymal cells transfected with siRNA for Trp53.
source: Furthermore, expression of both Runx2 and Sp7 was also significantly reduced in the palatal mesenchymal cells transfected with siRNA for Trp53 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C), which indicated that the downregulated expression of Trp53 in the palatal mesenchymal cells resulted in differentiation defects, which were also observed in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Nutlin-3 treatment successfully rescued the cleft palate in three out of five Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
source: In contrast, Nutlin-3 treatment successfully rescued the cleft palate in three out of five Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice (Figure 4G–R).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 4G–R.

claim: The protein level of P53 was successfully restored in the Nutlin-3-treated group.
source: Western blot analysis showed that the protein level of P53 was successfully restored in the Nutlin-3-treated group (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Downregulation of Trp53 in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice plays an essential role in the palatal defects.
source: This result further revealed that downregulation of Trp53 in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice plays an essential role in the palatal defects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from Nutlin-3 rescue experiments.

claim: The genetic interaction between Kdm6b and Trp53 is important for the development of post-migratory CNCCs.
source: The genetic interaction between Kdm6b and Trp53 is important for the development of post-migratory CNCCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from rescue experiments and expression data.

claim: Loss of Kdm6b in CNC-derived cells resulted in accumulation of H3K27me3 in the nucleus of CNC-derived palatal mesenchymal cells.
source: To investigate whether Kdm6b regulates the expression of Trp53 through modifying the level of H3K27me3, we first examined the status of H3K27me3 in our samples and found that loss of Kdm6b in CNC-derived cells resulted in accumulation of H3K27me3 in the nucleus of CNC-derived palatal mesenchymal cells (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A–D.

claim: The level of H3K27me3 was increased in the palatal region of Kdm6b mutant mice.
source: Furthermore, immunoblotting revealed that the level of H3K27me3 was increased in the palatal region of Kdm6b mutant mice (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: No obvious differences were observed in either the distribution of Ezh1+ cells or the EZH1 protein level between control and Kdm6b mutant mice.
source: We found no obvious differences in either the distribution of Ezh1+ cells or the EZH1 protein level between control and Kdm6b mutant mice (Figure 5F–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization and Western blot data shown in Figure 5F–J.

claim: No dramatic changes were observed in either the distribution of EZH2+ cells or its protein level between control and Kdm6b mutant mice.
source: Similarly, no dramatic changes were observed in either the distribution of EZH2+ cells or its protein level between control and Kdm6b mutant mice (Figure 5K–O).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 5K–O.

claim: Increased H3K27me3 in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice was mainly caused by loss of Kdm6b in CNC-derived cells.
source: These results indicated that increased H3K27me3 in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice was mainly caused by loss of Kdm6b in CNC-derived cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of changes in EZH1 and EZH2 expression.

claim: In Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl;Ezh2fl/+ mice, a rescue of the abnormal accumulation of H3K27me3 was observed.
source: In Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl;Ezh2fl/+ mice, we observed a rescue of the abnormal accumulation of H3K27me3 (Figure 5P–V).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 5P–V.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of Ezh2 successfully rescued the cleft palate phenotype observed in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice with 70% efficiency.
source: More importantly, haploinsufficiency of Ezh2 in this model successfully rescued the cleft palate phenotype observed in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice (Figure 6A–O) with 70% efficiency (N = 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by CT imaging and histological analysis shown in Figure 6A–O.

claim: Both the palatine processes of the maxilla and palatine bone were restored in the Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl;Ezh2fl/+ mice.
source: CT scanning showed that both the palatine processes of the maxilla and palatine bone were restored in the Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl;Ezh2fl/+ mice (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by CT imaging data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: Both EdU+ and RUNX2+ cells were restored to normal levels in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl;Ezh2fl/+ mice.
source: Furthermore, both EdU+ and RUNX2+ cells were restored to normal levels in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl;Ezh2fl/+ mice (Figure 7A–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling and RUNX2 immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A–H.

claim: An antagonistic interaction between the histone demethylase KDM6B and methyltransferase EZH2 that modulates H3K27me3 is essential for palatogenesis.
source: These results suggested that an antagonistic interaction between the histone demethylase KDM6B and methyltransferase EZH2 that modulates H3K27me3 is essential for palatogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from rescue experiments showing restoration of phenotypes by Ezh2 haploinsufficiency.

claim: Deposition of H3K27me3 significantly increased at the promoter of Trp53 in the palatal region of Kdm6b mutant mice.
source: A primer set was designed at 1127 bp upstream of Trp53 exon 1, and the results showed that deposition of H3K27me3 significantly increased at the promoter of Trp53 in the palatal region of Kdm6b mutant mice, while this increase was dampened in the Ezh2 haploinsufficiency model (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of Ezh2 in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl;Ezh2fl/+ mice was able to restore the decreased expression of Trp53 observed in the CNC-derived palatal mesenchyme of Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
source: Meanwhile, haplosufficiency of Ezh2 in Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl;Ezh2fl/+ mice was able to restore the decreased expression of Trp53 observed in the CNC-derived palatal mesenchyme of Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice (Figure 8B–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8B–H.

claim: Kdm6b and Ezh2 co-regulate expression of Trp53 through H3K27me3.
source: These data suggested that Kdm6b and Ezh2 co-regulate expression of Trp53 through H3K27me3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from ChIP-qPCR and expression data showing H3K27me3 changes at Trp53 promoter.

claim: Deposition of KDM6B significantly increased at the promoter of Trp53 in the palatal region.
source: To further reveal whether KDM6B regulates the expression of Trp53 directly, we performed ChIP-qPCR using KDM6B antibody and found that deposition of KDM6B significantly increased at the promoter of Trp53 in the palatal region (Figure 8I).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8I.

claim: Increased expression of Trp53 could be detected only in the group transfected with Kdm6b-overexpressing plasmid, not in the group transfected with Kdm6a-overexpressing plasmid.
source: Increased expression of Trp53 could be detected only in the group transfected with Kdm6b-overexpressing plasmid (Figure 8J and K, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8J and K, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Kdm6b has an essential and unique role in activating Trp53 during palatogenesis.
source: These results indicated that Kdm6b has an essential and unique role in activating Trp53 during palatogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from overexpression experiments showing Kdm6b but not Kdm6a can activate Trp53.

claim: The promoter region of Trp53 was accessible to members of the E2F transcription factor family (E2F4 and E2F6) and transcription factor TFDP1.
source: Through motif analysis, we found that the promoter region of Trp53 was accessible to members of the E2F transcription factor family (E2F4 and E2F6) and transcription factor TFDP1 (also known as Dp1), a binding partner of E2F family members (Figure 8L, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq motif analysis shown in Figure 8L, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Binding of TFDP1 to the promoter region of Trp53 decreased in the Kdm6b mutant mice.
source: ChIP-qPCR using palate tissue at E13.5 also revealed that binding of TFDP1 to the promoter region of Trp53 decreased in the Kdm6b mutant mice (Figure 8M).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8M.

claim: TFDP1+ cells were distributed in the palatal region and co-expressed with Trp53 and Kdm6b.
source: Immunohistochemistry analysis showed that TFDP1+ cells were distributed in the palatal region and co-expressed with Trp53 and Kdm6b (Figure 8N and O).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8N and O.

claim: The expression level and distribution of TFDP1 were not affected in the palatal mesenchyme of Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice.
source: Meanwhile, the expression level and distribution of TFDP1 were not affected in the palatal mesenchyme of Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice (Figure 8P, Figure 8—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and immunostaining data shown in Figure 8P, Figure 8—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: Tfdp1 is not a downstream target of Kdm6b.
source: These data indicated that Tfdp1 is not a downstream target of Kdm6b.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of changes in TFDP1 expression in Kdm6b mutant mice.

claim: The expression of Trp53 was decreased in cells treated with siRNA for Tfdp1.
source: qPCR revealed that the expression of Trp53 was decreased in cells treated with siRNA for Tfdp1 (Figure 8Q, Figure 8—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8Q, Figure 8—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Trp53 is a direct downstream target of Tfdp1.
source: This data further indicated that Trp53 is a direct downstream target of Tfdp1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from siRNA knockdown experiments showing decreased Trp53 expression.

claim: The expression of Trp53 increased in cells from control mice but not in cells from Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice when transfected with Tfdp1-overexpressing plasmid.
source: To reveal the function of Kdm6b-Tfdp1 interaction in the regulation of Trp53 during palatogenesis, we transfected palatal mesenchymal cells with Tfdp1-overexpressing plasmid and found that the expression of Trp53 increased in the cells from control mice but not in the cells from Wnt1Cre;Kdm6bfl/fl mice (Figure 8R and S, Figure 8—figure supplement 1J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8R and S, Figure 8—figure supplement 1J and K.

claim: Kdm6b is specifically required and plays an essential role in the activation of Trp53 through interaction with Tfdp1 during palatogenesis.
source: This result suggested that Kdm6b is specifically required and plays an essential role in the activation of Trp53 through interaction with Tfdp1 during palatogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from overexpression experiments showing Tfdp1 cannot activate Trp53 without Kdm6b.

claim: KDM6B and TFDP1 are involved in the same complex.
source: We performed co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) experiments and found that KDM6B and TFDP1 were indeed involved in the same complex (Figure 8T).
evidence: The claim is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 8T.

claim: KDM6B and TFDP1 work together to activate Trp53 expression in the palatal mesenchyme and play an important role in regulating palatogenesis.
source: Collectively, these data suggested that KDM6B and TFDP1 work together to activate Trp53 expression in the palatal mesenchyme and play an important role in regulating palatogenesis (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including ChIP-qPCR, Co-IP, and functional studies.

claim: The function of Kdm6b in activating Trp53 in palatal mesenchymal cells cannot be compensated for by the closely related histone demethylase Kdm6a.
source: More importantly, the function of Kdm6b in activating Trp53 in these cells cannot be compensated for by the closely related histone demethylase Kdm6a.
evidence: The claim is supported by overexpression experiments showing Kdm6a cannot activate Trp53 in Kdm6b mutant cells.

claim: Epigenetic regulation plays extensive roles in diseases and development.
source: Epigenetic regulation plays extensive roles in diseases and development.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: Disruption of epigenetic regulation not only increases the risk of cancer, but can also cause various developmental defects.
source: Disruption of epigenetic regulation not only increases the risk of cancer, but can also cause various developmental defects.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: Kdm6b plays an essential role in cranial neural crest development.
source: Our study shows that Kdm6b plays an essential role in cranial neural crest development, and loss of Kdm6b disturbs P53 pathway-mediated activity, leading to complete cleft palate along with cell proliferation and differentiation defects in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mouse models showing cleft palate and cellular defects.

claim: Loss of Kdm6b disturbs P53 pathway-mediated activity, leading to complete cleft palate along with cell proliferation and differentiation defects in mice.
source: Our study shows that Kdm6b plays an essential role in cranial neural crest development, and loss of Kdm6b disturbs P53 pathway-mediated activity, leading to complete cleft palate along with cell proliferation and differentiation defects in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing P53 pathway disruption and associated phenotypes.

claim: Activity of H3K27me3 on the promoter of Trp53 is antagonistically controlled by Kdm6b and Ezh2 in cranial neural crest cells.
source: Furthermore, activity of H3K27me3 on the promoter of Trp53 is antagonistically controlled by Kdm6b, and Ezh2 in cranial neural crest cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing H3K27me3 changes at Trp53 promoter and rescue experiments.

claim: Without Kdm6b, the transcription factor TFDP1, which normally binds to the promoter of Trp53, cannot activate Trp53 expression in palatal mesenchymal cells.
source: More importantly, without Kdm6b, the transcription factor TFDP1, which normally binds to the promoter of Trp53, cannot activate Trp53 expression in palatal mesenchymal cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR and overexpression experiments showing TFDP1 requires Kdm6b to activate Trp53.

claim: Palatogenesis is a complex process known to be regulated by multiple genetic regulatory mechanisms, including several signaling pathways (BMP, SHH, WNT, FGF, and TGFβ) and different transcription factors (such as Msx1, Sox9, Lhx6/8, Dlx5, and Shox2).
source: Palatogenesis is a complex process known to be regulated by multiple genetic regulatory mechanisms, including several signaling pathways (BMP, SHH, WNT, FGF, and TGFβ) and different transcription factors (such as Msx1, Sox9, Lhx6/8, Dlx5, and Shox2) (Satokata and Maas, 1994; Yu et al., 2005; Chai and Maxson, 2006; Levi et al., 2006; Cobourne et al., 2009; Lee and Saint-Jeannet, 2011; Nakamura et al., 2011; Bush and Jiang, 2012; He and Chen, 2012; Parada and Chai, 2012; Xu et al., 2016; Reynolds et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge from multiple cited studies.

claim: Environmental effects can contribute to orofacial defects.
source: However, environmental effects can also contribute to orofacial defects, which lends further support to the notion that genetic factors are not sufficient to fully explain the etiology of many birth defects (Dixon et al., 2011; Roessler et al., 2012; Seelan et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge from cited studies.

claim: Heterozygous mutation of SATB2 can cause cleft palate in patients.
source: Furthermore, case studies have revealed that heterozygous mutation of a chromatin-remodeling factor, SATB2, and variation in DNA methylation can cause cleft palate in patients (Leoyklang et al., 2007; Chandrasekharan and Ramanathan, 2014; Young et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on case studies cited in the text.

claim: Variation in DNA methylation can cause cleft palate in patients.
source: Furthermore, case studies have revealed that heterozygous mutation of a chromatin-remodeling factor, SATB2, and variation in DNA methylation can cause cleft palate in patients (Leoyklang et al., 2007; Chandrasekharan and Ramanathan, 2014; Young et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on case studies cited in the text.

claim: The contribution of cranial neural crest cells (CNCCs) is critical to palate mesenchyme formation.
source: The contribution of cranial neural crest cells (CNCCs) is critical to palate mesenchyme formation.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about neural crest development.
